narrative:
The model predicted a 68% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles, respectively, among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your family income bracket was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. Coming from an upper-middle-income background (the most common bracket among accepted students) slightly improved the model’s outlook. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 32 and undergraduate GPA of 2.90 were also below the averages of accepted students, reinforcing the same concern.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, or consider retaking the bar exam after targeted preparation. Many students in similar situations succeed on a second attempt or by addressing the specific skill gaps these rankings highlight.
